anthropic.title: Anthropic
anthropic.body:
Anthropic is an American artificial intelligence company, led by [[dario-amodei|Dario Amodei]], that develops frontier AI models and has publicly advocated stronger safety guardrails on advanced systems.[{n}]

## Role in the open-source AI dispute

In the July 2026 fight over [[open-source-artificial-intelligence|open-source artificial intelligence]], Anthropic was grouped with [[openai|OpenAI]] as a company that has "generally supported stronger safeguards for frontier AI systems," in contrast to open-source advocates who argue that excessive regulation would entrench incumbent firms and reduce America's ability to compete globally.[{n}] Venture capitalist [[chamath-palihapitiya|Chamath Palihapitiya]] warned that a government ban on open-source AI would tank the market and crater both Anthropic and OpenAI.[{n}] Trump-aligned technologists, including members of the administration's Innovation Council, argued that restricting open-source development would benefit foreign rivals, particularly [[china|China]], while letting a small number of companies control advanced AI capabilities.[{n}]

## Badlands commentary

[[burning-bright|Burning Bright]] argued that the push by [[sam-altman|Sam Altman]] and Amodei for government regulation was an attempt to slow and control the industry's acceleration, placing it "in collectivist, oligarchic hands," and that the two men are therefore "retardants" rather than "accelerants" to the AI agenda.[{n}] He cited former White House AI and Crypto Czar [[david-sacks|David Sacks]] as stating that Anthropic and OpenAI seek regulation chiefly to stave off competitors, and Commerce Secretary [[howard-lutnick|Howard Lutnick]] as saying the administration aims to "protect open source AI."[{n}]

dario-amodei.title: Dario Amodei
dario-amodei.body:
Dario Amodei is the chief executive of [[anthropic|Anthropic]] and, with [[sam-altman|Sam Altman]] of [[openai|OpenAI]], one of the two figures most identified with the industry campaign for government regulation of frontier AI systems.[{n}]

## Open-source AI dispute

In July 2026, as Trump-aligned technologists escalated a public argument over restrictions on [[open-source-artificial-intelligence|open-source artificial intelligence]], Amodei's Anthropic was characterized as favoring stronger safeguards on frontier models, while open-source advocates argued such rules would entrench incumbents and weaken the United States against foreign competitors, above all [[china|China]].[{n}] [[burning-bright|Burning Bright]] argued that the Amodei-Altman regulatory push was designed to slow and control AI acceleration rather than supercharge an American Age of Abundance, making them "retardants" to the AI agenda, and cited [[david-sacks|David Sacks]] as making the same case publicly.[{n}]

david-sacks.title: David Sacks
david-sacks.body:
David Sacks is an American venture capitalist and technology executive who served as White House AI and Crypto Czar in the second [[donald-trump|Trump]] administration; the Badlands Brief renders his surname as "Sachs."[{n}]

## Open-source AI shadow war

In late July 2026 Sacks argued publicly that [[openai|OpenAI]] and [[anthropic|Anthropic]] pursue government regulation of frontier AI out of competitive self-interest rather than safety.[{n}] [[burning-bright|Burning Bright]] wrote that Sacks laid out "almost beat for beat" his own framing from the previous week, "openly stating that he believes they're only seeking government regulation so they can stave off competitors."[{n}] The remarks were cited alongside Commerce Secretary [[howard-lutnick|Howard Lutnick]]'s reported statement that the administration aims to "protect open source AI" as evidence that the [[open-source-artificial-intelligence|open-source AI]] dispute had become an explicit policy fight in the administration's orbit.[{n}]

chamath-palihapitiya.title: Chamath Palihapitiya
chamath-palihapitiya.body:
Chamath Palihapitiya is an American venture capitalist and technology investor associated with the Trump-aligned segment of Silicon Valley finance.[{n}]

## Open-source AI warning

In July 2026 Palihapitiya was among the venture capitalists and technology executives who criticized proposals that could limit [[open-source-artificial-intelligence|open-source artificial intelligence]] models, warning that a government ban on open-source AI would tank the market and crater both [[anthropic|Anthropic]] and [[openai|OpenAI]] — a claim reported by [[zerohedge|ZeroHedge]] and echoed in [[axios|Axios]] coverage.[{n}] His intervention was cited alongside members of the administration's Innovation Council in arguments that open-source development accelerates innovation, broadens American technological leadership, and prevents a small number of companies from controlling advanced AI capabilities.[{n}]

oversight-project.title: Oversight Project
oversight-project.body:
The Oversight Project is an American government-accountability and litigation organization that pursues transparency actions against federal officials and agencies.[{n}]

## Release of the Biden ghostwriter tapes

In July 2026 the Oversight Project published more than seventy hours of recordings of [[joe-biden|Joe Biden]] speaking with his memoir ghostwriter [[mark-zwonitzer|Mark Zwonitzer]], obtained during special counsel [[robert-hur|Robert Hur]]'s classified documents probe.[{n}] The 2016 and 2017 recordings were released after a lengthy legal fight in which Biden's attorneys spent months attempting to block publication before abandoning their lawsuit; a judge accepted the dismissal on the preceding Monday.[{n}] In them Biden warns, "Some of this may be classified … So, be careful," and elsewhere says, "this is classified."[{n}] The organization's Vice President of Litigation, [[jeff-clark|Jeff Clark]], said the recordings should force a full reexamination of the decision to give Biden a pass for keeping and disclosing classified information.[{n}]

pew-research-center.title: Pew Research Center
pew-research-center.body:
The Pew Research Center is an American nonpartisan polling and social science research organization whose surveys are widely cited in political and foreign-policy reporting.[{n}]

## Polling on Israel and Netanyahu

In the July 2026 debate over whether Prime Minister [[benjamin-netanyahu|Benjamin Netanyahu]] had damaged [[israel|Israel]]'s standing with the American public, Pew findings served as the empirical basis of the argument: unfavorable views of Israel and declining confidence in Netanyahu had risen since 2022, with opinion worsening across demographic groups and among younger voters in both major parties.[{n}] Commentators used these results to argue that Israel had shifted from a largely bipartisan issue in American politics to an increasingly polarizing one.[{n}]

indira-talwani.title: Indira Talwani
indira-talwani.body:
Talwani is the federal district judge whose injunction against President [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]]'s executive order on election administration was left intact by a federal appeals court in July 2026; the Badlands Brief refers to her only by surname.[{n}]

## Election order injunction

Her order blocked key portions of the executive order from being enforced in 23 Democrat-led states while litigation continued.[{n}] The order had directed the [[department-of-homeland-security|Department of Homeland Security]] to compile lists of confirmed citizens eligible to vote, instructed the [[united-states-postal-service|US Postal Service]] to set new standards for mail-in ballots, and directed the [[department-of-justice|Justice Department]] to prioritize investigations of officials issuing federal ballots to ineligible people.[{n}] The appeals court denied the DOJ's request to lift the injunction; [[ashe-in-america|Ashe in America]] noted the decision "does not settle the underlying dispute over presidential power but keeps Talwani's injunction intact while the case winds through the courts, a delay that could push final resolution dangerously close to the midterms."[{n}] Badlands commentary called the outcome the work of a "very silly judge," arguing that if neither the states nor the President may direct the USPS, no actor would hold its decision rights.[{n}]

open-source-artificial-intelligence.title: Open-Source Artificial Intelligence
open-source-artificial-intelligence.body:
Open-source artificial intelligence refers to AI systems whose code, and in the "open-weight" form whose trained parameters, are released publicly so anyone may run, study, modify and build on them. By mid-2026 whether the US government should restrict such releases had become a central technology-policy dispute of the second [[donald-trump|Trump]] administration.[{n}]

## The 2026 policy fight

Leading figures in the Trump-aligned technology and venture capital community described the competition over open-source AI as a strategic battle with major national security and economic implications, arguing that restrictions would weaken US competitiveness while benefiting foreign rivals, particularly [[china|China]].[{n}] The debate intensified after venture capitalists and executives — including [[chamath-palihapitiya|Chamath Palihapitiya]] and members of the administration's Innovation Council — criticized proposals limiting open models, contending that open development accelerates innovation, broadens American technological leadership, and prevents a small number of companies from controlling advanced AI capabilities.[{n}] The dispute exposed a divide within the industry: [[openai|OpenAI]] and [[anthropic|Anthropic]] have generally supported stronger safeguards for frontier systems, while open-model advocates argue excessive regulation entrenches incumbents.[{n}]

## The AI Shadow War thesis

[[burning-bright|Burning Bright]] argued on the Devolution Power Hour that the issue bears on "alternatively starting or stopping the American Golden Age" more than almost anything else, while going unnoticed in the [[truth-community|Truth Community]].[{n}] He held that the regulatory campaign by [[sam-altman|Sam Altman]] and [[dario-amodei|Dario Amodei]] sought to slow and control acceleration and place AI "in collectivist, oligarchic hands."[{n}] He cited three confirmations: [[david-sacks|David Sacks]] saying the labs want regulation to stave off competitors; [[howard-lutnick|Howard Lutnick]] saying the administration aims to "protect open source AI"; and China timing open-weight releases that accelerate the industry while blunting Western attempts to slow it, granting Trump narrative shielding.[{n}] His conclusion: China is "actually HELPING protect the future of an open-source, open-weight, FREE AI world," and "Good thing Trump and [[xi-jinping|Xi]] are Sovereign Bros."[{n}]
